Juicebox details come from Juicebox's public pricing, product and documentation pages, checked October 14, 2026.

Pin is built for recruiting teams that want sourcing, outreach and interview scheduling in one product, and it is trusted by 2,000+ organizations and 20,000+ users. SHRM found AI use in HR tasks reached 43% of organizations in 2025, up from 26% in 2024. Some comparisons call Pin a solo-recruiter tool. This one checks Pin and Juicebox against their current public pages.

Pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that automates the top of the funnel, from sourcing and outreach to interview scheduling, for solo recruiters, agencies and in-house teams. Juicebox (PeopleGPT) is an AI sourcing platform that pairs natural-language candidate search with outreach sequences, ATS and CRM integrations, and add-on AI agents. For a longer feature-by-feature breakdown, see Pin's Pin vs Juicebox comparison.

No. Pin has a one-seat Solo plan at $99 a month on annual billing, and solo recruiters and small agencies use it. But Pin's team features and pricing are built for multiple users:

Juicebox does team work too. According to its pricing page (October 2026), Growth lets you invite up to five teammates to collaborate on searches, shortlists and outreach, and Business adds hiring-manager seats, usage analytics and ATS or CRM integration. Pin's team pages describe hiring managers, sourcers and closers sharing one view of the req.

Pin says it searches 850M+ profiles across multiple sources, including North America and Europe, aggregated from professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, open-source contributions, patents, academic publications and the broader web. You can search in plain language, paste a job description, upload ideal résumés or import a role from your ATS. Each ranked candidate gets a fit score and an AI-written reason, and the model learns from accept and reject feedback across the team.

Juicebox offers natural-language search over a stated 800 million profiles from "30+" sources, and its AI Spotlight also explains why a candidate matches. It adds three data features worth knowing about:

Pin lists Talent Insights on Professional and Business too. Profile counts say little about quality, so run the same roles in both. If you are also pricing LinkedIn's tool, see LinkedIn Recruiter alternatives.

Pin runs multi-channel sequences across email, LinkedIn and SMS: automated email steps plus AI-drafted LinkedIn and SMS tasks in the same sequence, which the recruiter sends. Pin reports those sequences deliver 5x better response rates than industry averages, benchmarked against LinkedIn's published 10-25% InMail reply rates. Pin drafts each message from the candidate's own profile signals and calibrates to your writing voice. Sequences adapt per candidate, any reply pauses the sequence, and every channel stays in one thread. The Free plan is email-only, multi-channel sequences start on Solo, and Professional includes five mailboxes per user.

Juicebox's outreach page (October 2026) describes "email, calls, and social touches in one sequence," automatic stop on reply and analytics by step and channel. Growth includes three mailboxes per seat, Business six. Its agents page describes agent outreach as email only.

No. Pin's AI recruiting agent has two modes. In Assist, you approve each step. In Autopilot, the agent sources, screens and ranks, drafts outreach, sends the email steps, follows up on silence, schedules interviews and updates the ATS. LinkedIn and SMS steps queue as tasks with AI-drafted messages that the recruiter sends. Pin assists recruiters and never replaces them: closing and offers stay human. Human-in-the-loop guardrails apply, and every action appears in a feed. Pin saves recruiters 12 hours per week on sourcing and outreach combined, according to Pin's 2026 user survey across 2,000+ organizations and 20,000+ users.

It is also steerable. Pin asks clarifying questions about the brief, such as "Is remote considered?", and you refine in plain language. Josh Volinsky, Co-Founder of Synergy Search, says: "Pin makes sourcing candidates so natural and I love how you can just talk to it like it's a recruiter on your team and it goes hunting."

Pin's MCP server lets you work from Claude Desktop, Claude Code, ChatGPT or Codex: start searches, review candidates, tune the search in plain language and keep per-job memory. Pin says "You still approve every accept, reject, and outreach." It is free on every paid plan.

Juicebox's agents are steerable too. According to its agents page (October 2026), you recalibrate by chatting with the agent, with autonomy from fully hands-off to manual checkpoints at shortlist or sequencing. #10641. How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

In the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation. In short: for the first output token (prefill step), the entire prompt needs to be processed, which can be parallelized efficiently and can saturate GPU utilization. For all later output tokens (decode steps), only a single additional token needs to be processed, which is less compute-intensive but must be done sequentially. When many requests are processed concurrently, any strategy that aims for low latency needs to run prefill steps for newly arriving requests while the decode steps of previously scheduled requests are still ongoing. Concurrent processing of new as well as running requests therefore requires careful balancing between the prefill and decode stages, which presents two major challenges, which we will discuss in the following. One is a readily solvable issue, while the other one constitutes a more fundamental flaw.

Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests. For prefill, however, this approach does not work. Because of the parallelized processing of all prompt tokens, a single prefill step can already saturate GPU utilization. Consequently, in the default chunked-prefill strategy of vLLM, each prefill chunk contains only prompt tokens of a single request. The next request in line has to wait until the previous prefill phase has been finished before its own prefill phase can start.

This sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue. (Note that the sequential processing of prefills is the default characteristic of chunked-prefill and only appears when there already is a concurrent request in its decode phase; hence the name "partial prefill".)

Unfortunately, this challenge can neither be solved with vLLM-side priority scheduling (see the first article of this series) nor with a more sophisticated upstream scheduler. The reason is that the long prompt can be scheduled before any subsequent requests exist, so there is nothing the scheduler could wait for.

A straightforward solution would be to process prefill chunks of different requests in parallel. This might not be resource-optimized, as single-request prefill chunks could already saturate compute-power. Any additional prefill executed in parallel would likely prolong the prefill duration a bit and slow down any concurrent decode-requests even further. This would be acceptable if it reduced the latency of short requests and made the system appear more responsive. This approach fails, however, when the next request in line has a long prompt too. In such a case, two compute-intensive prefills would be batched together and result in a severe slowdown.

In one of the latest vLLM updates, an improved strategy has been implemented: it allows for parallel prefills of different requests but with a limit to the number of concurrently processed long prompt requests. An example configuration could enable batching of prefills for four requests, but only one of them may be longer than 10,000 prompt tokens. With such a configuration, the behavior for longer requests is still the same as before: long prompts are processed sequentially. Short requests, however, no longer need to wait for the long prefill of a previous request to finish; short prompts can take a fast lane. These requests no longer suffer from long waiting times and show much lower time-to-first-token metrics.

Of course, parallel prefills can only reduce waiting times; but the time-per-output-token remains elevated during the concurrent long-prefill operation. In this regard, request-parallel prefills show the same behavior and performance as standard chunked-prefill, just with a shorter time-to-first-token.

Whenever prefill and decode of different requests are executed in the same GPU operation, it takes longer than for an isolated decode step. The user experiences an interruption or a slowing down of the token generation by a subsequent request. In particular, a single request with a long prompt is sufficient to slow down all previously scheduled requests that are already in their decode phases.

This is a fundamental flaw in the concurrent processing of prefill and decode on the same GPUs, because there is little you can do:

The difference between ideal concurrent processing (which would be no different from isolated requests), actual concurrent processing, and a disaggregated prefill strategy is shown by the following measurements:

Separating prefill and decode eliminates the slowing-down of token generation in presence of other requests to a large extent, which makes it a very attractive strategy. It comes at the price of a second full-size vLLM deployment (e.g. for Llama-3.3-70B, you would need four H100 GPUs for a prefill worker and another four H100 GPUs for a decode worker if you wanted to support a maximum context length of 130k tokens). Another disadvantage is the uneven GPU utilization: because prefill is compute-intensive but decode is not, the prefill worker will likely saturate GPU utilization before the decode worker does. On the other hand, large clusters could consist of different numbers of prefill and decode workers (depending on load patterns), in order to optimize resource utilization.

Disaggregated prefill is not intended to increase total throughput, rather total "goodput" (i.e. the rate of requests that satisfy latency targets). Consequently, it is not the best use of GPU resources if your application is not sensitive to latency of individual requests.

Another caveat: the disaggregated prefill feature in vLLM is still experimental, and some optimizations and features are not accessible yet. For example, there are currently lower limits on context length, and the decode worker doesn't use CUDA graphs consistently, causing the slower decode of the long-prompt request in the figure above. Fortunately, these are not fundamental obstacles and are likely going to be solved in future versions of vLLM.

#10639. Microsoft now lets you turn off AI search results completely in Bing

Microsoft is giving Bing users the option to turn off AI-generated answers in their search results, allowing them to browse the internet without being shown AI summaries.

AI has become a major part of online searches in recent years, with companies like Microsoft and Google using the technology to generate quick answers to questions instead of simply providing links to websites.

While this can be useful for quickly finding information, not everyone wants AI to be involved in their searches at all times.

Now, Microsoft is giving people more control over how they use Bing, with two simple ways to remove AI-generated answers from their results.

In a November 11 announcement, Microsoft revealed a new browser extension called Bing AI Search Choice, which lets users switch AI-generated answers on or off.

Once installed, the extension adds a toggle that can be used to choose between traditional search results and AI-powered summaries.

The setting applies to all searches made through Bing, meaning users won’t have to change their preferences every time they look something up.

However, the extension is currently only available for Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, and installing it will also make Bing your default search engine.

For those who don’t want to install anything, simply adding “-ai” to the end of a Bing search will remove AI-generated answers from the results. For example, searching for “best games of 2026 -ai” will bring up results without the usual AI summaries.

Microsoft explained that the feature is about giving people the freedom to decide how they want to search.

New Microsoft patent could use AI to alter speech and lip movements in real time

How to turn off AI in Google search results

Bing AI is now available to everyone and it just got smarter

“AI is doing powerful things for search, and our research shows users want to have the option to choose whether or not AI is involved in every session,” the company said.

“Sometimes a quick AI-generated summary is exactly what you need. Other times, you’d rather scan the results, compare sources and decide for yourself what information to trust.”

The browser extension is currently in preview, meaning Microsoft could make further changes based on user feedback.

#10638. How to Optimize AI-Generated Images for Faster Websites

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated images are becoming a common part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product illustrations, landing pages, blog posts, and digital interfaces. However, generating an image is only one part of the process. Before publishing it, developers need to ensure that the image loads quickly, displays correctly across devices, and maintains its visual quality.

Large image files can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay the appearance of important content. These problems can affect user experience and website performance, particularly on mobile devices and slower internet connections.

A reliable image optimization workflow helps address these challenges. By selecting appropriate dimensions, choosing efficient image formats, automating image processing, and implementing responsive delivery, developers can improve loading performance without sacrificing visual quality.

This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques and development tools.

Images often account for a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. Uploading large, unoptimized images can make pages slower and increase the amount of data visitors need to download.

Several common problems contribute to poor image performance:

Incorrect dimensions waste bandwidth on smaller screens.

Missing image dimensions can cause unexpected layout shifts.

Poor responsive configuration can make browsers download unnecessarily large images.

Incorrect loading priorities can delay important visual content.

These issues can affect Core Web Vitals, including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how quickly the largest visible content element appears.

For developers, image optimization should therefore be part of the website development workflow rather than a final task performed immediately before publication.

Before optimizing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small interface graphic.

For example, a website might use the following dimensions:

These dimensions are examples rather than fixed requirements. The appropriate size depends on the website layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

When preparing source visuals, developers can explore different AI image generation options and consider how the generated images will fit their intended layouts.

Once the image is ready, keep a high-quality master file. This allows developers to create smaller versions for different screen sizes without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

Avoid enlarging small images unnecessarily because upscaling can introduce blur and visible artifacts.

Choosing the right format can reduce image size while preserving acceptable visual quality.

Three commonly used formats are AVIF, WebP, and JPEG.

AVIF: Often provides efficient compression for photographs and detailed illustrations. It can significantly reduce file sizes, although encoding may take longer.

WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation. It offers broad browser support and is suitable for many website images.

JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and situations where compatibility with older software or systems is important.

PNG is appropriate for certain lossless graphics, screenshots, and images that require transparency. However, it can produce unnecessarily large files when used for photographic content.

No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare file sizes and inspect visual quality before selecting the final output.

A practical approach is to generate AVIF and WebP versions and provide a JPEG fallback where necessary.

Manually resizing and converting images becomes time-consuming when a website contains dozens or hundreds of visual assets.

Automation makes the process more consistent. Developers can use Sharp, a Node.js image-processing library, to resize images, convert formats, and generate multiple versions from a single source file.

Next, create a file named build-images.mjs:

The script creates multiple image sizes in both WebP and AVIF formats.

The quality settings are starting points, not universal recommendations. Developers should adjust them after checking the resulting file sizes and visual details.

This approach is particularly useful for content-heavy websites, product catalogs, and applications that publish images regularly.

Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on the visitor's screen and the space available in the layout.

HTML provides two important attributes for this purpose: srcset and sizes.

The srcset attribute lists the available image files and their widths. The sizes attribute describes how wide the image is expected to appear at different viewport sizes.

In this example, the image is expected to occupy approximately 720 pixels on wider screens and nearly the full viewport width on smaller screens.

The browser uses this information to choose an appropriate image candidate.

One common mistake is setting sizes="100vw" for an image that occupies only a small part of the page. This can encourage the browser to download a larger file than necessary.

Always ensure that the sizes attribute reflects the actual website layout.

The HTML picture element allows developers to provide multiple image formats and a fallback option.

The browser selects a supported format, while the img element provides the fallback image and alternative text.

Developers should verify that every referenced file exists and that its dimensions match the intended layout.

The picture element can also support different crops for desktop and mobile devices. This is useful when a wide banner needs a separate composition for smaller screens.

Images without defined dimensions can cause content to move while the browser loads the file. This behavior contributes to Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Including width and height attributes helps browsers reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

For responsive layouts, developers can use CSS:

This allows images to scale within their containers while maintaining their proportions.

Images below the initial viewport can generally use native lazy loading:

However, the main hero image should not normally be lazy-loaded when it is responsible for LCP. Delaying an important above-the-fold image can make the page appear slower.

Where appropriate, developers can use fetchpriority="high" for the main image to help the browser prioritize its download.

The correct strategy depends on the image's position and importance within the page.

Image optimization involves more than file size and dimensions. Developers should also consider accessibility, file organization, and metadata.

Alternative text helps people using screen readers understand meaningful images. It should describe the image's purpose in the context of the page.

Decorative images that provide no useful information should generally use an empty alt attribute.

File names should also be descriptive. Names such as home-office-sunrise.webp are easier to understand and maintain than generic names such as image-final-v3.png.

Metadata requires additional consideration. Image-processing tools may remove metadata by default to reduce file size. This can include information that a project needs to preserve, depending on its requirements.

Before removing metadata, developers should review whether the website or client requires attribution, provenance information, or other embedded details.

After implementing an optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

Chrome DevTools provides useful information about image requests.

Open Developer Tools and select the Network panel.

Resize the viewport or use device emulation.

Check whether the browser downloads appropriately sized images.

Developers can also inspect the image selected by the browser through the console:

This returns the current image URL selected for that element.

For websites with multiple images, inspect the relevant elements individually.

Finally, run an audit using Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. These tools can identify issues involving oversized images, image formats, loading priorities, and other performance factors.

Image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, JavaScript, and third-party scripts can also influence loading speed.

Several mistakes can reduce the effectiveness of an image optimization workflow:

Uploading original images without checking their dimensions.

Assuming one format always produces the smallest file.

Omitting the sizes attribute from responsive images.

Lazy-loading important above-the-fold images.

Applying excessive compression and damaging visual details.

Removing metadata without checking project requirements.

Measuring file size without inspecting the final visual quality.

A consistent testing process helps identify these issues before they affect visitors.

No. AVIF often provides efficient compression, but the results depend on the image, encoding settings, and quality requirements. Comparing both formats is the best way to choose an appropriate option.

Four to six sizes may be sufficient for many websites. The ideal number depends on the layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

Yes. Reducing the size of the main content image, providing responsive versions, and avoiding unnecessary loading delays can improve LCP when that image is the largest contentful element.

No. Lazy loading is useful for images outside the initial viewport. Important images near the top of the page should generally load promptly.

The fundamental techniques are the same as those used for conventional images. However, AI-generated visuals may contain complex textures, gradients, and fine details that require careful inspection after compression.

AI-generated images can improve website design and make it easier to create custom visual content. However, efficient delivery requires more than exporting an image and uploading it to a website.

Developers should choose suitable dimensions, compare modern image formats, automate processing, and implement responsive image delivery. Including image dimensions helps prevent layout shifts, while appropriate loading priorities can improve the experience for visitors.

By testing images across different devices and reviewing their actual performance, development teams can maintain visual quality while reducing unnecessary downloads.

A repeatable optimization workflow makes it easier to publish new visuals without sacrificing website speed, accessibility, or reliability.

#10636. (LoRA) Fine-Tuning FLUX.1-dev on Consumer Hardware

In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance. We saw how bitsandbytes, torchao, and others reduce memory footprints for generating images.

Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them. Therefore, in this post, we tackle efficient fine-tuning of these models with peak memory use under ~10 GB of VRAM on a single GPU. This post will guide you through fine-tuning FLUX.1-dev using QLoRA with the diffusers library. We'll showcase results from an NVIDIA RTX 4090. We'll also highlight how FP8 training with torchao can further optimize speed on compatible hardware.

We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.

The model consists of three main components:

In our QLoRA approach, we focus exclusively on fine-tuning the transformer component. The text encoders and VAE remain frozen throughout training.

We used a diffusers training script (slightly modified from here designed for DreamBooth-style LoRA fine-tuning of FLUX models. Also, a shortened version to reproduce the results in this blogpost (and used in the Google Colab) is available here. Let's examine the crucial parts for QLoRA and memory efficiency:

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Deep Dive: LoRA makes model training more efficient by keeping track of the weight updates with low-rank matrices. Instead of updating the full weight matrix W W W, LoRA learns two smaller matrices A A A and B B B. The update to the weights for the model is ΔW=BA \Delta W = B A ΔW=BA, where A∈Rr×k A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} B∈Rd×r. The number r r r (called rank) is much smaller than the original dimensions, which means less parameters to update. Lastly, α \alpha α is a scaling factor for the LoRA activations. This affects how much LoRA affects the updates, and is often set to the same value as the r r r or a multiple of it. It helps balance the influence of the pre-trained model and the LoRA adapter. For a general introduction to the concept, check out our previous blog post: Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning.

QLoRA: The Efficiency Powerhouse: QLoRA enhances LoRA by first loading the pre-trained base model in a quantized format (typically 4-bit via bitsandbytes), drastically cutting the base model's memory footprint. It then trains LoRA adapters (usually in FP16/BF16) on top of this quantized base. This dramatically lowers the VRAM needed to hold the base model.

For instance, in the DreamBooth training script for HiDream 4-bit quantization with bitsandbytes reduces the peak memory usage of a LoRA fine-tune from ~60GB down to ~37GB with negligible-to-none quality degradation. The very same principle is what we apply here to fine-tune FLUX.1 on a consumer-grade hardware.

8-bit Optimizer (AdamW): Standard AdamW optimizer maintains first and second moment estimates for each parameter in 32-bit (FP32), which consumes a lot of memory. The 8-bit AdamW uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer states in 8-bit precision, while maintaining training stability. This technique can reduce optimizer memory usage by ~75% compared to standard FP32 AdamW. Enabling it in the script is straightforward:

Gradient Checkpointing: During forward pass, intermediate activations are typically stored for backward pass gradient computation. Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory by only storing certain checkpoint activations and recomputing others during backpropagation.

Cache Latents: This optimization technique pre-processes all training images through the VAE encoder before the beginning of the training. It stores the resulting latent representations in memory. During the training, instead of encoding images on-the-fly, the cached latents are directly used. This approach offers two main benefits:

Only these LoRA parameters become trainable.

Before we launch the QLoRA fine-tune we can save a huge chunk of VRAM and wall-clock time by caching outputs of text encoders once.

At training time the dataloader simply reads the cached embeddings instead of re-encoding the caption, so the CLIP/T5 encoder never has to sit in GPU memory.

By combining this with cached VAE latents (--cache_latents) you whittle the active model down to just the quantized transformer + LoRA adapters, keeping the whole fine-tune comfortably under 10 GB of GPU memory.

For this demonstration, we leveraged an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM) to explore its performance. The full training command using accelerate is shown below.

Configuration for RTX 4090: On our RTX 4090, we used a train_batch_size of 1, gradient_accumulation_steps of 4, mixed_precision="bf16", gradient_checkpointing=True, use_8bit_adam=True, a LoRA rank of 4, and resolution of 512x768. Latents were cached with cache_latents=True.

Training Time (RTX 4090): Fine-tuning for 700 steps on the Alphonse Mucha dataset took approximately 41 minutes on the RTX 4090 with train_batch_size of 1 and resolution of 512x768.

Output Quality: The ultimate measure is the generated art. Here are samples from our QLoRA fine-tuned model on the derekl35/alphonse-mucha-style dataset:

This table compares the primary bf16 precision results. The goal of the fine-tuning was to teach the model the distinct style of Alphonse Mucha.

The fine-tuned model nicely captured Mucha's iconic art nouveau style, evident in the decorative motifs and distinct color palette. The QLoRA process maintained excellent fidelity while learning the new style.

The results are nearly identical, showing that QLoRA performs effectively with both fp16 and bf16 mixed precision.

For users with NVIDIA GPUs possessing compute capability 8.9 or greater (such as the H100, RTX 4090), even greater speed efficiencies can be achieved by leveraging FP8 training via the torchao library.

We fine-tuned FLUX.1-dev LoRA on an H100 SXM GPU slightly modifieddiffusers-torchao training scripts. The following command was used:

The training run had a peak memory usage of 36.57 GB and completed in approximately 20 minutes.

Qualitative results from this FP8 fine-tuned model are also available:

Key steps to enable FP8 training with torchao involve:

For a more detailed guide and code snippets, please refer to this gist and the diffusers-torchao repository.

After training your LoRA adapters, you have two main approaches for inference.

One approach is to load your trained LoRA adapters on top of the base model.

For when you want maximum efficiency with a single style, you can merge the LoRA weights into the base model.

While we showcased results on an RTX 4090, the same code can be run on more accessible hardware like the T4 GPU available in Google Colab for free.

On a T4, you can expect the fine-tuning process to take significantly longer around 4 hours for the same number of steps. This is a trade-off for accessibility, but it makes custom fine-tuning possible without high-end hardware. Be mindful of usage limits if running on Colab, as a 4-hour training run might push them.

QLoRA, coupled with the diffusers library, significantly democratizes the ability to customize state-of-the-art models like FLUX.1-dev. As demonstrated on an RTX 4090, efficient fine-tuning is well within reach, yielding high-quality stylistic adaptations. Furthermore, for users with the latest NVIDIA hardware, torchao enables even faster training through FP8 precision.

Sharing your fine-tuned LoRA adapters is a fantastic way to contribute to the open-source community. It allows others to easily try out your styles, build on your work, and helps create a vibrant ecosystem of creative AI tools.

If you've trained a LoRA for FLUX.1-dev, we encourage you to share it. The easiest way is to add the --push_to_hub flag to the training script. Alternatively, if you have already trained a model and want to upload it, you can use the following snippet.

Check out our Mucha LoRA and the TorchAO FP8 LoRA. You can find both, plus other adapters, in this collection.

#10635. Man buys two-bedroom apartment for just $1.70 in China’s Black Friday-style sale

A man in China has purchased an apartment for just $1.70 during a shopping promotion event, and it’s just as absurd as it sounds.

Shopping sales usually mean saving money on a shiny new TV or picking up a discounted game or two, but one lucky man in China took money-saving to an entirely new level by purchasing a two-bedroom apartment for just $1.70.

The property was sold through Chinese bidding platform Alibaba Auction as part of the country’s Double 11 event, an annual shopping festival that’s similar to Black Friday.

Located in Heilongjiang province in northeastern China, the seventh-floor apartment measures 68 square metres (roughly 732 square feet) and has two bedrooms.

According to the South China Morning Post, bidding started at one yuan (around $0.15) and was capped at 11 yuan (around $1.65). While 1,677 bidders took part, it was an anonymous shopper from eastern China’s Jiangsu-Zhejiang region who managed to secure the property.

Despite landing a new home for less than a cup of coffee, the buyer revealed he has no plans to relocate. Instead, he intends to use the two-bedroom property as a place to stay during winter holidays.

While the man may have purchased the apartment for $1.70, he will need to pay around 2,000 yuan (approximately $300) in deed taxes to complete the title transfer. SCMP also cited a warning from Beijing Jinsu Law Firm, which said buyers considering ultra-cheap properties should check for issues such as unclear ownership, unpaid taxes, and outstanding fees.

Either way, securing an apartment for just $1.70 puts it right next to owning an entire Japanese castle for $64,000 (yes, this is a real thing).

#10634. Transformers backend integration in SGLang

Hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data. Its simplicity, flexibility, and expansive model zoo make it a powerful tool for rapid development.

But once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical. That’s where SGLang comes in.

Designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend. This means you can pair the flexibility of transformers with the raw performance of SGLang.

Let’s dive into what this integration enables and how you can use it.

SGLang now supports Hugging Face transformers as a backend, letting you run any transformers-compatible model with high-performance inference out of the box.

No native support needed — SGLang automatically falls back to Transformers when needed, or you can set impl="transformers" explicitly.

Let’s walk through a simple text generation example with meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct to compare both approaches.

transformers library is great for experimentation, small-scale tasks and training, but it's not optimized for high-volume or low-latency scenarios.

SGLang takes a different track, prioritizing efficiency with features like RadixAttention (a memory-efficient attention mechanism). Inference with SGLang is noticeably faster and more resource-efficient, especially under load. Here’s the same task in SGlang using an offline engine:

Or you can spin a server and send requests:

Note that SGLang also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, making it a drop-in replacement for external services.

With the new transformers backend integration, SGLang can now automatically fall back to using transformers models it doesn’t natively support. This means in practice:

This unlocks faster inference and optimized deployment (e.g enabling RadixAttention) without sacrificing the simplicity and versatility of transformers ecosystem.

Note that specifying the impl parameter is optional. If the model is not natively supported by SGLang, it switches to transformers implementation on its own.

Any model on the Hugging Face Hub that works with transformers using trust_remote_code=True and properly implements attention is compatible with SGLang. You can find the exact requirements in the official documentation. If your custom model meets these criteria, all you need to do is set trust_remote_code=True when loading it.

Kyutai Team’s Helium isn’t yet natively supported by SGLang. This is where transformers backend shines, enabling optimized inference without waiting for native support.

There are several key areas we are actively working on to enhance this integration:

Performance Improvements: transformer models currently lag behind the native integration in terms of performance.Our primary objective is to optimize and narrow this gap.

VLM Integration: we are also working toward adding support for Vision-Language Models (VLM) to broaden the range of capabilities and use cases.

#10633. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy controversy

Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned after 33 years leading the company, with an interim replacement taking over immediately.

The announcement on November 12 comes just four days after Nvidia launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation involving a suspected Chinese spy.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has stepped down as president, CEO, and a member of the board of directors.

Nvidia confirmed that Colette Kress, its executive vice president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.

Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013 and has overseen its financial operations during a period of significant growth. She will retain her existing responsibilities while serving as interim CEO, with the company considering both internal and external candidates for the permanent position.

The leadership change follows reports that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

The two are not related, and the allegations prompted Nvidia’s board to announce an independent investigation on November 8, overseen by outside legal counsel.

At the time, Nvidia said it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised. The company also expressed confidence in Huang’s leadership and confirmed that he would cooperate with the investigation.

Huang subsequently acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, apologizing to his family and colleagues while maintaining his commitment to the company.

The controversy also attracted attention from US lawmakers, with three House committee chairs requesting a closed-door briefing with Huang on November 18 to discuss his interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s security procedures.

Nvidia launches independent investigation into CEO after reports of suspected Chinese spy link

Nvidia stopping RTX 5090 production to focus on AI graphics cards: Report

Nvidia CEO warns US of dangers surrounding Chinese chip war

China’s Foreign Ministry has rejected the espionage allegations, while Singaporean authorities have said they did not identify Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Shortly after the investigation, it was reported that Huang had a second affair with an executive from the company, and on November 12, Reuters reported a third alleged affair with a second employee.

Nvidia’s November 12 announcement did not address the status of its investigation or whether Huang would continue cooperating following his departure.

Alongside Kress’s appointment, Nvidia announced that Harvey C. Jones would become the company’s first-ever chair of the board.

Jones, who has more than 30 years of experience in the technology industry, said the company expects its operations and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Jones said.

“She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

Kress also addressed her appointment, thanking Huang for his contributions to Nvidia over the past three decades.

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” she said.

“We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Huang’s departure comes as Nvidia faces increased scrutiny over its leadership and business dealings with China, with its advanced AI chips remaining subject to US export restrictions.

#10632. How to Test AI-Generated Content Before It Reaches Your Users

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most teams now ship something an AI helped write: help-center articles, product descriptions, release notes, even code comments. The draft appears in seconds, and that speed is the trap. Nobody tests it the way they would test a new feature, so mistakes slip through that a quick review would have caught.

This guide is about the other side of AI testing. Instead of using AI to test your software, you test what AI hands you. Here is a simple routine that fits into a normal publishing or release process.

AI writing sounds confident whether or not it is right. A model can invent a statistic (researchers call this hallucination and have documented it across many text-generation systems), quote a feature your product does not have, or describe a setting that was renamed two releases ago. The sentence reads smoothly, so the error hides in plain sight.

Traditional QA does not cover this. A unit test tells you the page loads. It says nothing about whether the claim on the page is true. That gap is where most AI-related incidents begin.

1. Define what "good" means before you generate anything. Write down the audience, the claims you are willing to make and the sources you trust. A short brief makes the output easier to judge, because you are comparing it with something concrete.

2. Check every factual claim. Highlight each number, name and statement of fact, then verify it against a primary source. Google's own guidance on generative AI content tells publishers to fact-check AI output, including titles, descriptions and alt text, before publishing. If you cannot confirm a claim in a minute or two, cut it or rewrite it as something you can support.

3. Test the instructions. For tutorials and how-to content, follow the steps exactly as written on a clean machine or account. Commands that fail and menus that no longer exist show up immediately this way.

4. Review the voice. Replace vague phrases with specifics from your own experience: a real customer question, a real error message, a real number from your analytics. This is also what separates useful content from filler.

5. Keep a human owner. Every piece should have a named person who approved it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework makes the same point at organization level: people stay accountable for how AI is used and evaluated. If something goes wrong later, you know who to ask and where to fix it.

Some teams also run drafts through an AI detector. That can be useful as a prompt for a closer look, for example when freelancers or vendors deliver work and you want to know how much of it was machine-generated. A high score is a reason to read more carefully. It is not proof of anything, and it should never decide an outcome on its own, because detectors make mistakes in both directions. A Stanford study found that GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, and short texts are easy to misjudge too. If you want a quick second opinion on a draft, a tool like Tester AI can give you a starting point for that conversation.

Review works best when it is not optional. A few small habits make it stick.

Treating the first draft as finished. It is a starting point. Plan time for review the same way you plan time for writing.

Reviewing for grammar only. Clean sentences are not evidence of correct content. Check meaning first and polish second.

Letting the tool grade its own work. Asking the same model to confirm its answer rarely catches real errors. Use a source or a person.

Skipping legal and brand review. Generated text can echo existing material or make promises your company cannot keep. Anything customer-facing deserves a second pair of eyes.

AI can save hours of drafting, but speed only helps if the result is trustworthy. Treat generated content like code from a new contributor: useful, often good, and always reviewed before it goes live. A short routine of defining quality, verifying facts, testing instructions and keeping a human owner will catch most problems before your users do.

Do I need to test AI-generated content if a human edits it? Yes. Editing for style does not confirm that the facts are correct. Verify claims separately from polishing the wording.

How long should a review take? For a typical article, expect roughly the time it takes to read it twice plus a few minutes per factual claim. Reviews are faster when the brief and sources are prepared in advance.

Can an AI detector prove that text was written by a machine? No. Detectors estimate likelihood, and they can be wrong. Use the result as a signal for human review, never as the final decision.

What should I check first? Start with numbers, names, dates and anything a customer could act on, such as prices, steps or legal statements. Those carry the highest risk if they are wrong.

#10631. Gemma 3n fully available in the open-source ecosystem!

Gemma 3n was announced as a preview during Google I/O. The on-device community got really excited, because this is a model designed from the ground up to run locally on your hardware. On top of that, it’s natively multimodal, supporting image, text, audio, and video inputs 🤯

Today, Gemma 3n is finally available on the most used open source libraries. This includes transformers & timm, MLX, llama.cpp (text inputs), transformers.js, ollama, Google AI Edge, and others.

This post quickly goes through practical snippets to demonstrate how to use the model with these libraries, and how easy it is to fine-tune it for other domains.

Two model sizes have been released today, with two variants (base and instruct) each. The model names follow a non-standard nomenclature: they are called gemma-3n-E2B and gemma-3n-E4B. The E preceding the parameter count stands for Effective. Their actual parameter counts are 5B and 8B, respectively, but thanks to improvements in memory efficiency, they manage to only need 2B and 4B in VRAM (GPU memory).

These models, therefore, behave like 2B and 4B in terms of hardware support, but they punch over 2B/4B in terms of quality. The E2B model can run in as little as 2GB of GPU RAM, while E4B can run with just 3GB of GPU RAM.

In addition to the language decoder, Gemma 3n uses an audio encoder and a vision encoder. We highlight their main features below, and describe how they have been added to transformers and timm, as they are the reference for other implementations.

The easiest way to vibe check the model is with the dedicated Hugging Face Space for the model. You can try out different prompts, with different modalities, here.

Install the latest version of timm (for the vision encoder) and transformers to run inference, or if you want to fine tune it.

The easiest way to start using Gemma 3n is by using the pipeline abstraction in transformers:

Initialize the model and the processor from the Hub, and write the model_generation function that takes care of processing the prompts and running the inference on the model.

Since the model supports all modalities as inputs, here's a brief code explanation of how you can use them via transformers.

Support for videos is done as a collection of frames of images

Gemma 3n comes with day 0 support for MLX across all 3 modalities. Make sure to upgrade your mlx-vlm installation.

In addition to MLX, Gemma 3n (text only) works out of the box with llama.cpp. Make sure to install llama.cpp/ Ollama from source.

Check out the Installation instruction for llama.cpp here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/install.md

Finally, we are also releasing ONNX weights for the gemma-3n-E2B-it model variant, enabling flexible deployment across diverse runtimes and platforms. For JavaScript developers, Gemma3n has been integrated into Transformers.js and is available as of version 3.6.0.

For more information on how to run the model with these libraries, check out the usage section in the model card.

Given the size of the model, it’s pretty convenient to fine-tune it for specific downstream tasks across modalities. To make it easier for you to fine-tune the model, we’ve created a simple notebook that allows you to experiment on a free Google Colab!

We also provide a dedicated notebook for fine-tuning on audio tasks, so you can easily adapt the model to your speech datasets and benchmarks!

With this release, we also introduce the Hugging Face Gemma Recipes repository. One will find notebooks and scripts to run the models and fine tune them.

We would love for you to use the Gemma family of models and add more recipes to it! Feel free to open Issues and create Pull Requests to the repository.

We are always excited to host Google and their Gemma family of models. We hope the community will get together and make the most of these models. Multimodal, small sized, and highly capable, make a great model release!

If you want to discuss the models in more detail, go ahead and start a discussion right below this blog post. We will be more than happy to help!

A huge thanks to Arthur, Cyril, Raushan, Lysandre, and everyone at Hugging Face who took care of the integration and made it available to the community!

#10630. Viral Cowboy who took his horse on bus responds after Detroit launches investigation

A horse owner has responded after a viral video showed them taking their horse onto a bus, and even the city is investigating.

When you’re using public transport, it isn’t a shock to see a dog sitting next to its owner, or other pets being transported in carry cases. These are pretty common sights for regular bus and train riders.

However, on November 9, the internet’s attention was caught by a viral video of two horses being led onto a bus in Detroit. In the clip, which was filmed from across the street, the two riders approached the door while holding their horses on a leash.

Both horses and riders were able to get on board the bus briefly, but they didn’t stick around for long. That left the woman recording the scene, Elessia Drew, in disbelief. “This is crazy,” she said.

The video has been reposted across social media since Drew first posted it to Facebook, attracting millions of views.

Jordan Williams, the horse’s owner, told WXYZ that he helped his horse on board for a funny video, but has taken them on buses before. “We walked on, and I must tell you the buses are a lot smaller than they used to be, or I may have been a little bigger,” he said.

“The point is just to bring light to… like there are cowboys that look like us.”

However, the Detroit Department of Transport has said they are taking the “taking appropriate steps to address this incident” as it is “not consistent with DDOT policy and potentially creates an unsafe and uncomfortable ride for our passengers.”

Williams told WXYZ that he hopes they “look at it like a joke like everyone else,” rather than taking any action.

#10629. Quantum computer breakthrough tracks qubit fluctuations in real time

Researchers at the Niels Bohr Institute have significantly increased how quickly changes in delicate quantum states can be detected inside a qubit. By combining commercially available hardware with new adaptive measurement techniques, the team can now observe rapid shifts in qubit behavior that were previously impossible to see.

Qubits are the fundamental units of quantum computers, which scientists hope will one day outperform today's most powerful machines. But qubits are extremely sensitive. The materials used to build them often contain tiny defects that scientists still do not fully understand. These microscopic imperfections can shift position hundreds of times per second. As they move, they alter how quickly a qubit loses energy and with it valuable quantum information.

Until recently, standard testing methods took up to a minute to measure qubit performance. That was far too slow to capture these rapid fluctuations. Instead, researchers could only determine an average energy loss rate, masking the true and often unstable behavior of the qubit.

It is somewhat like asking a strong workhorse to pull a plow while obstacles constantly appear in its path faster than anyone can react. The animal may be capable, but unpredictable disruptions make the job much harder.

A research team from the Niels Bohr Institute's Center for Quantum Devices and the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme, led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Fabrizio Berritta, developed a real time adaptive measurement system that tracks changes in the qubit energy loss (relaxation) rate as they occur. The project involved collaboration with scientists from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Leiden University, and Chalmers University.

The new approach relies on a fast classical controller that updates its estimate of a qubit's relaxation rate within milliseconds. This matches the natural speed of the fluctuations themselves, rather than lagging seconds or minutes behind as older methods did.

To achieve this, the team used a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), a type of classical processor designed for extremely rapid operations. By running the experiment directly on the FPGA, they could quickly generate a "best guess" of how fast the qubit was losing energy using only a few measurements. This eliminated the need for slower data transfers to a conventional computer.

Programming FPGAs for such specialized tasks can be challenging. Even so, the researchers succeeded in updating the controller's internal Bayesian model after every single qubit measurement. That allowed the system to continually refine its understanding of the qubit's condition in real time.

As a result, the controller now keeps pace with the qubit's changing environment. Measurements and adjustments happen on nearly the same timescale as the fluctuations themselves, making the system roughly one hundred times faster than previously demonstrated.

The work also revealed something new. Scientists did not previously know just how quickly fluctuations occur in superconducting qubits. These experiments have now provided that insight.

Commercial Quantum Hardware Meets Advanced Control

FPGAs have long been used in other scientific and engineering fields. In this case, the researchers used a commercially available FPGA based controller from Quantum Machines called the OPX1000. The system can be programmed in a language similar to Python, which many physicists already use, making it more accessible to research groups worldwide.

The integration of this controller with advanced quantum hardware was made possible through close collaboration between the Niels Bohr Institute research group led by Associate Professor Morten Kjaergaard and Chalmers University, where the quantum processing unit was designed and fabricated. "The controller enables very tight integration between logic, measurements and feedforward: these components made our experiment possible," says Morten Kjærgaard.

Why Real Time Calibration Matters for Quantum Computers

Quantum technologies promise powerful new capabilities, though practical large scale quantum computers are still under development. Progress often comes incrementally, but occasionally major steps forward occur.

By uncovering these previously hidden dynamics, the findings reshape how scientists think about testing and calibrating superconducting quantum processors. With current materials and manufacturing methods, moving toward real time monitoring and adjustment appears essential for improving reliability. The results also highlight the importance of partnerships between academic research and industry, along with creative uses of available technology.

"Nowadays, in quantum processing units in general, the overall performance is not determined by the best qubits, but by the worst ones: those are the ones we need to focus on. The surprise from our work is that a 'good' qubit can turn into a 'bad' one in fractions of a second, rather than minutes or hours.

"With our algorithm, the fast control hardware can pinpoint which qubit is 'good' or 'bad' basically in real time. We can also gather useful statistics on the 'bad` qubits in seconds instead of hours or days.

"We still cannot explain a large fraction of the fluctuations we observe. Understanding and controlling the physics behind such fluctuations in qubit properties will be necessary for scaling quantum processors to a useful size," Fabrizio says.

Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

With its powerful OCR capabilities and efficient performance on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, this model delivers industry-leading accuracy for text and table extraction, as well as chart, diagram, and table parsing. Whether you’re automating financial document processing or improving business intelligence workflows, Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for fast, scalable deployments.

Check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL! Users can also post-train the model further with their own datasets using NVIDIA NeMo.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR). With its high accuracy, low model footprint, and multimodal capabilities, Llama Nemotron Nano VL enables the seamless extraction and understanding of information from complex documents. This includes PDFs, images, tables, charts, formulas, and diagrams, making it an ideal solution for automating document workflows across various industries like finance, healthcare, legal, and government.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL demonstrates exceptional accuracy on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, which tests models on real-world OCR and document understanding tasks. These tasks include text recognition, table extraction, and element parsing across various document types. The model’s advanced capabilities enable it to deliver better performance than current leading VLMs in real-world enterprise scenarios.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL builds upon Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and C-RADIOv2-VLM-H, a Vision Transformer (ViT) that serves as the backbone for visual feature extraction. This allows the model to handle a wide variety of visual elements in documents, including charts, graphs, and other complex visual representations.

C-RADIOv2-VLM-H Vision Transformer (ViT): The core visual understanding component of the model, C-RADIO allows for high-resolution processing of documents containing complex visual elements. This serves as a vision backbone, excelling across visual domains and enabling the model to process multi-image understanding with high resolution. This technology underpins the model’s ability to handle complex documents containing visual elements such as images, diagrams, charts, and tables.

C-RADIO is trained on multi-resolution data using multiple distillation techniques. Multiplicative noise was applied to our weights during training to improve generalization.

Llama Nemotron VL further adopts a design that dynamically aggregates encoded patch features, enabling support for high-resolution input without sacrificing spatial continuity. This strategy efficiently processes documents with arbitrary aspect ratios while preserving both local detail and global context. It enables fine-grained analysis of dense visual content—such as small fonts, multi-column layouts, and intricate charts—without compromising computational efficiency or coverage. The model can also preserve the information better and have less distortion, due to the innovation in high-resolution tiling.

By empowering Llama-3.1 8B LLM with this strong vision foundation, Llama Nemotron Nano VL delivers unparalleled accuracy in parsing and interpreting documents.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using several OSS datasets along with data from NVIDIA’s VLM-based OCR solution, NeMo Retriever Parse. This provides capabilities in text and table parsing, along with grounding, enabling the Llama Nemotron Nano VL to perform at an industry-leading level in document understanding tasks. Synthetic table extraction datasets that were used for training this OCR solution were also used for training Llama Nemotron Nano VL 8B VLM to enable more optimal table understanding and extraction.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL excels in tasks like text recognition and visual reasoning, and demonstrates advanced chart and diagram understanding capabilities. Llama Nemotron Nano VL allows for predicting bounding box coordinates in normalized space to enable grounding like tasks and text-referring.

This strong performance is underpinned by high-quality in-domain data combined with a diverse training distribution across document types, languages, and layouts. A robust data strategy ensures coverage across challenging use cases through selective curation, targeted augmentation, and formatting techniques that clarify task intent and reduce ambiguity—resulting in models that generalize effectively to real-world applications.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL undergoes a two-stage training regimen: pre-training followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The initial pre-training phase focuses on achieving cross-modal alignment between the language and vision domains. This is accomplished through the training of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector, which serves as an interface between the two modalities.

For the training process, Llama Nemotron Nano VL leverages a comprehensive and diverse collection of datasets. This aggregated dataset, comprising a total of ~1.5M samples, includes publicly available, synthetically generated, as well as internally curated datasets. A summary of the datasets utilized during the pre-training stage is presented in Figure 1.

In the Supervised Fine-Tuning stage, Llama-Nemotron-Nano-VL is trained end-to-end on a combination of synthetic, public, and internally curated datasets. The data encompasses a wide spectrum of tasks, including but not limited to: OCR, text grounding, table parsing, and general document-based VQA.

The document understanding capabilities of Llama Nemotron Nano VL can be largely attributed to the OCR-focused SFT data blend. Besides simple OCR, many of the datasets involve tasks such as predicting the correct reading order, reconstructing markdown formatting along with semantic classes (such as Captions, Titles, Section headers) and bounding boxes of individual text blocks. The model is also trained to parse mathematical formulas in LaTeX format and to extract tables in LaTeX, HTML, or markdown formats, depending on the prompt.

To ensure robustness across various domains, we apply affine and photometric augmentations to the document images. To improve the table and chart parsing performance further, we enable swapping of tables and charts embedded into the full-page documents between the datasets. This enables the model to handle diverse document layouts and structures.

A large portion of the internally-created datasets are based on Nemo Retriever Parse training data. These include NVPDFTex - a collection of arxiv documents with ground-truth labels consisting of formatted text in reading order, with bounding boxes and semantic classes of text, as well as LaTeX tables and equations; Common Crawl pdfs that are labeled by human annotators; rendered text from Wikipedia with markdown formatting and tables, as well as a number of synthetic datasets targeted at improving table parsing capabilities and dense OCR. In addition, the training blend includes a number of publicly-available datasets, such as DocLayNet, FinTabNet and PubTables-1M, in which we refine the groundtruth labels.

Figure 2 below shows the task distribution of the training data. As can be seen, a significant portion of the training samples involve OCR along with grounding and table parsing, as well as OCR-adjacent VQA tasks.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using NVIDIA Megatron and utilizes efficient Transformer implementations in NVIDIA Transformer Engine. For multimodal dataloading, we use Megatron Energon. We provide example Megatron training and inference scripts along with hyperparameters and other instructions to enable custom training of VLMs.

To ensure the output is formatted precisely as you need, we recommend including detailed instructions within your prompts. We've provided some examples below to illustrate how this works for various tasks:

OCRBench v2 is an advanced benchmark designed to evaluate OCR models across a diverse range of real-world document types and layouts. It includes over 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs to rigorously assess a model’s capabilities in visual text localization, table parsing, diagram reasoning and key-value extraction.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL outperforms other VLMs on this benchmark and also achieves strong accuracies in benchmarks such as ChartQA and AI2D, making it a compelling option for enterprises aiming to automate document workflows such as:

Its combination of high accuracy, strong layout aware reasoning, and efficient deployment on a single GPU makes it an ideal choice for large-scale enterprise automation.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for various document processing tasks across multiple industries. Here are some of the key use cases where the model excels:

Automating the extraction of line items, totals, dates, and other key data points from invoices and receipts. This is crucial for accounting, ERP integration, and expense management.

Extracting structured data from passports, IDs, and tax forms for regulatory compliance and KYC processes.

Automatically identifying key clauses, dates, and obligations in legal documents.

Extracting patient data, claim information, and policy details from medical records and insurance forms.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL provides developers with the tools to automate document processing workflows at scale. It is available through the NVIDIA NIM API and for download on Hugging Face, where you can begin building production-ready document understanding applications. Users can also use NVIDIA NeMo to finetune the model on their own dataset.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a powerful multimodal model designed to meet the demanding needs of intelligent document processing in modern enterprises. Whether you are processing invoices, contracts, or compliance documents, this model provides the accuracy, efficiency, and scalability required for high-performance document understanding.

For a hands-on experience, check out our tutorial on invoice and receipt document intelligence, and start leveraging the full power of Llama Nemotron Nano VL today.
